snippet.textDisplay:
Just lost my mom at almost 94. I'm happy for her, because she had bad heart disease and dementia, but sad for me because at 69 I still had my mom. I will say her dementia made her a stranger to me. The sharp, witty, wise mom I had was replaced by a confused person who would sometimes do bizarre and dangerous things. At some level she knew she was losing it and she was very distressed about it.
She was cared for in her own home till she died. I guess that as a geriatric nurse for 40 tears and a Christian I know that our time on earth is limited. RIP, Mom. I hope somewhere you are that beautiful compassionate person who raised me once again.

snippet.textDisplay: I was watching Amapour & they had a segment on just this subject. I am a nurse of many years. I work in gerontology well over 15 to 18 years. It is a field that is BIG money but a very sad environment for those medically, mentally sick individuals. I have firm point of view for myself. It is not going to be as the mainstream as everyone else goes. To observe these unfortunate elderly individuals on a day to day basis is excruciating even for a medical worker. Some families are great and the others are just the opposite. Most individuals are unable to pay for long term care, the same goes for long term insurance. This is a concern that will NOT go away anytime soon. Families do need to make better end of life decisions than is what is currently going on.

snippet.textDisplay: I'm in my 40s. Closer to 50 than I'd like to admit. My parents died 12 days apart in January of 2024. They were married 58 years, together for 63. snippet.textDisplay: Thank you for this video.  It's great to see you and many people in the comments share your situations.  I thought I was alone.  This year has been very taxing and disheartening.  I am the youngest child and in my 30's.  Both parents are seniors.  My dad had back surgery and while recovering had complications with catheters and UTI's.  My mom has had heart complications .  I have a brother and sister but they haven't helped much.  I have been physically and emotionally drained.  The calvary is not coming.  It's been non stop to the point where I have not taking good care of myself.  I have gained 40lbs and have not had much sleep.  My mom with heart complications has memory issues now and from time to time has a completely different and hostile personality.  My dad is recovering in hospital.  We have some home health care.  But it's been nonstop.  As a single person with no kids I feel like this is the closest I have to taking care of kids.  I am there for them but it can break a spirit when they begin to resist help and become resentful to the one person who is taking care of their well being.  Hopefully this storm will pass and they can get better.

snippet.textDisplay: My mother passed last year of vasculitis related dementia she was 90 stopped driving at 87 I took care of her at the family home my Dad passed 14 years before her of bladder cancer he passed at family home hospice came in 3 times a week check ups help bathe and help change bedding mom had a brain bleed then to hospital trauma to Hospice she was there 8 days was by both parents bedside          still miss them both mom  was very active and lucid during day but night was harder for her she stopped all meds blood pressure etc she lived the expected 5 years after diagnosis    was so happy I could care for her and she could stay in her own home.They do better in familiar surroundings than memory care.

snippet.textDisplay:
You’re not alone
I am 54 and my dad would be 94 but he passed a year ago. He had mild cognitive impairment, but essentially was tired and died peacefully. My mother is 93 and was sharp as attack until about two years ago. She had persistent, hypertension, and while she and dad lived at an assistant living, she was adamant to do as much for herself and dad as possible. I don’t think that’s a bad thing! She and I would put their med containers together every week of course I gave us another opportunity to spend time together
Navigating Drs’s appointments and advocating for their needs invest interests husband consuming, but it’s also part of my love language, I believe
I’m a registered nurse and while I’m the youngest kid I have been there, healthcare, power of attorney and advocate.
There is a lot to navigate!

snippet.textDisplay: I am 45 and I am currently the primary caregiver for my dad, he is 86. He has Alzheimers disease, aortic stenosis, metastases in lung and peritoneum from a colon carcinoma, chronic leukemia and paralysis of one vocal cord which makes him cough because he chokes food, beverages and even his saliva. Sounds like he could not be alive, but he is. We are having hard times, dealing with all his symptoms, like taste disorder (salt above all) and crazy side effecs from his meditation (hallucinations were the worst so far). My mom is also caring for my dad, but she is 76 and completely exhausted. I am working full time, luckily having the possibility to work from my parents house, where I moved in 4 weeks ago, leasing my own life behind. I am in perimenopause and try to take care of all, including myself. Fortunately I watched your videos, Dr. Haver, and I know what is going on in my body and my mind - and what I can do to feel better. Thank you so much for all the informations, it really helps. Navigating through this tough time is not easy, but we have good times and funny moments as well. And over all, the best feeling is, that I can help him in worse moments and ease his pain. Because I am here (and with the help of fantastic palliative experts!!!), he can be in his own house that he built with his own hands. That is his biggest wish. Take good care of yourselves!

snippet.textDisplay:
When my mom (with dementia) passed a few years ago, the worry and stress I had for her just transferred to…”I’m next with this horrible disease “…. “What can I do to prevent it, delay it, prepare for it, to ease this burden I see coming for my family?” The all consuming feelings just morph into a different focus. I wish I could tell you it gets easier with time but it only seems to shift. So much research wherever I have one free minute with one brain cell left. I imagine another angle of research being your focus for future internet presence. Not just surviving and thriving in menopause but next- research and avoiding dementia.
You got this! Thank You for All You Do for Womens Health.
